clinicalScope: Cirrhosis of the liver in adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Cirrhosis of the Liver
subject: Medicine
summary: Cirrhosis is advanced scarring of the liver that disrupts its function. It is common in East Africa due to viral hepatitis, alcohol, and schistosomiasis. Patients develop fluid overload, bleeding risk, and encephalopathy.

sections.p: Cirrhosis is irreversible replacement of normal liver parenchyma with fibrous tissue and regenerative nodules, leading to portal hypertension and loss of synthetic function.
b: Global prevalence ~1% but higher in sub‑Saharan Africa where chronic hepatitis B and alcohol are endemic.
In East Africa, hepatitis B infection accounts for ~50% of cirrhosis cases; alcohol and schistosomiasis each contribute 10‑20%.
Median age at presentation is 45‑55 y in low‑resource settings, younger than in high‑income countries.
Both sexes are affected; males have slightly higher rates due to higher alcohol use.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Identify the most prevalent aetiologies in the local context before rarer causes.
b: Chronic hepatitis B infection – vertical or early childhood acquisition.
Heavy alcohol consumption (>40 g/day for men, >20 g/day for women).
Schistosoma mansoni infection causing presinusoidal fibrosis.
Chronic hepatitis C (less common than B in East Africa).
Non‑alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) linked to obesity and diabetes.
Co‑infection with HIV accelerates fibrosis progression.

sections.p: Persistent hepatocyte injury triggers inflammation, stellate‑cell activation and collagen deposition, forming fibrous septa that bridge portal tracts and central veins.
b: Inflammatory cytokines (TNF‑α, IL‑6) activate hepatic stellate cells.
Activated stellate cells produce type I and III collagen → fibrosis.
Fibrous septa compress sinusoids → increased intra‑hepatic resistance → portal hypertension.
Peripheral vasodilatation (nitric oxide) leads to hyperdynamic circulation and renal sodium retention.
Reduced albumin synthesis causes hypo‑albuminaemia → ascites and edema.
Impaired detoxification raises ammonia → hepatic encephalopathy.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic early; decompensation produces characteristic signs.
b: Fatigue, anorexia, weight loss.
Jaundice (bilirubin > 2 mg/dL) when synthetic failure progresses.
Ascites – shifting dullness, abdominal girth increase.
Spider angiomas, palmar erythema, caput medusae.
Encephalopathy – asterixis, confusion, flapping tremor.
Upper‑GI bleeding – melena or hematemesis from esophageal varices.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical guide urgency and likely aetiology.
b: Ask about hepatitis B/C vaccination, prior transfusions, scarification, and HIV status.
Quantify alcohol intake (standard drinks per week).
Inquire about schistosomiasis exposure (freshwater contact).
Check for symptoms of portal hypertension: variceal bleeding, splenomegaly‑related cytopenias.
Examine for jaundice, spider nevi, palmar erythema, ascites (fluid wave), and asterixis.
Palpate liver edge – firm, nodular, and often not palpable due to atrophy.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic cirrhosis must be considered, especially when imaging is limited.
b: Congestive heart failure – transudative ascites, elevated JVP, cardiac murmur.
Nephrotic syndrome – massive proteinuria, peripheral edema, normal liver enzymes.
Budd‑Chiari syndrome – hepatic vein thrombosis, painful hepatomegaly, rapid ascites.
Advanced schistosomiasis without cirrhosis – presinusoidal portal hypertension, preserved synthetic function.
Autoimmune hepatitis – high IgG, positive auto‑antibodies, may respond to steroids.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise approach; note what to do when a test is unavailable.

t.b: Assesses synthetic function; < 3.5 g/dL indicates decompensation.
Reflects clotting factor production; INR > 1.5 suggests severe synthetic loss.
Elevated > 2 mg/dL signals cholestasis or hepatocellular failure.
Thrombocytopenia (< 150 ×10⁹/L) often due to splenic sequestration from portal hypertension.
Detects nodular liver surface, coarse echotexture, splenomegaly, and ascites; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs.
SAAG > 1.1 g/dL confirms portal‑hypertensive ascites; total protein < 2.5 g/dL suggests transudate.

t.a: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti‑HBc IgG
t.b: Positive results identify chronic HBV as the aetiology; treat with antivirals when available.
Rising creatinine (> 1.5 mg/dL) may herald hepatorenal syndrome.

sections.p: Child‑Pugh and MELD scores are the accepted tools; they guide prognosis and transplant referral.
b: Child‑Pugh: points for bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy; Class A (5‑6), B (7‑9), C (10‑15).
MELD: 3 × ln[bilirubin mg/dL] + 11 × ln[INR] + 9.6 × ln[creatinine mg/dL]; > 15 predicts 3‑month mortality.
In low‑resource settings, use Child‑Pugh when labs are limited; ascites and encephalopathy are key clinical inputs.
Decompensated cirrhosis = any Child‑Pugh B/C or presence of ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy, or hepatorenal syndrome.

sections.p: Local infections and co‑morbidities frequently worsen outcomes.
b: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) – gut aerobes (E. coli) invade ascitic fluid; SAAG > 1.1, neutrophils ≥ 250 cells/µL.
Hepatorenal syndrome – functional renal failure; treat with albumin and vasoconstrictors if available.
Co‑infection with HIV accelerates fibrosis and increases opportunistic infections.
Schistosomiasis may coexist, adding presinusoidal hypertension to sinusoidal disease.
Malnutrition worsens muscle wasting and encephalopathy risk.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control portal hypertension, and manage complications.
b: Eliminate alcohol completely; provide counseling and community support.
Antiviral therapy for chronic HBV (tenofovir/entecavir) when accessible; prioritize high‑viral‑load patients.
Low‑sodium diet (≤ 2 g/day) and fluid restriction (≤ 1.5 L) to limit ascites.
Screen for varices with endoscopy when possible; if unavailable, treat all patients with beta‑blockers.
Refer for liver transplantation evaluation when Child‑Pugh C or MELD > 15.

sections.p: Recognize emergencies that require immediate action.
b: Variceal hemorrhage – hematemesis or melena; give IV octreotide (if available) and arrange urgent endoscopic band ligation.
Hepatic encephalopathy – asterixis, confusion; give lactulose and correct precipitating factors.
Hepatorenal syndrome – rising creatinine, oliguria; give albumin and consider terlipressin (if available).
Acute decompensation with hypotension – treat with IV albumin and vasopressors; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.

sections.p: Pregnant women, children, and HIV‑positive patients need tailored care.
b: Pregnancy increases portal pressure; monitor for variceal bleed and avoid teratogenic drugs.
In HIV‑positive patients, prioritize HBV antiviral agents active against both viruses (tenofovir).
Patients with sickle cell disease may develop hepatic sequestration; differentiate from cirrhosis by rapid onset and pain.
Elderly patients have reduced renal reserve; adjust diuretic dosing and monitor electrolytes closely.

sections.p: Long‑term outcomes depend on aetiology control and complication management.
b: Annual ultrasound for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance when AFP testing unavailable.
Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B; give hepatitis B vaccine to all non‑immune adults.
Screen household contacts for HBV and provide prophylaxis.
Educate on safe water and schistosomiasis control (praziquantel).
Follow‑up every 3 months: clinical review, labs (bilirubin, albumin, INR), and ascites assessment.

sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings in low‑resource settings.
b: Normal transaminases do not exclude advanced fibrosis; rely on clinical signs and ultrasound.
Serum albumin may be low from malnutrition rather than liver failure alone.
SAAG can be falsely low if ascitic fluid is contaminated with urine or blood.
Platelet count may be low from HIV‑related marrow suppression, not just splenic sequestration.

whenToSeekHelp: Vomiting blood or black tarry stools
Sudden increase in abdominal girth with fever
New confusion, asterixis, or inability to stay awake
Rapidly falling blood pressure or urine output

faq.q: Why does cirrhosis cause low blood pressure despite fluid overload?
faq.a: Portal hypertension triggers nitric‑oxide‑mediated peripheral vasodilatation, reducing systemic vascular resistance.
Early fibrosis may regress if the cause is removed, but established cirrhosis is usually irreversible; transplantation is the only curative option.

faq.q: Is ascites always due to portal hypertension?
faq.a: In cirrhosis, most ascites is portal‑hypertensive; however, cardiac failure or nephrotic syndrome can produce similar fluid.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect decompensated cirrhosis in a patient with abdominal distension? — Look for shifting dullness, spider nevi, palmar erythema, asterixis, and low albumin; these indicate portal hypertension and synthetic failure.

A patient with known HBV presents with new ascites. Which investigation confirms portal‑hypertensive ascites and why? — Perform diagnostic paracentesis; SAAG > 1.1 g/dL confirms portal hypertension as the cause.

How does the Child‑Pugh score influence management decisions? — Class A may be observed; Class B warrants beta‑blockers and endoscopy; Class C requires transplant referral and aggressive complication control.

Why is spironolactone preferred over furosemide as first‑line diuretic in cirrhotic ascites? — It antagonises aldosterone‑mediated sodium retention, preserving potassium and addressing the underlying hyperaldosteronism.
A patient with cirrhosis develops fever and abdominal pain. What is your next step and why? — Obtain ascitic fluid for cell count; if neutrophils ≥ 250 cells/µL, start empiric cefotaxime for SBP.
Explain why non‑selective beta‑blockers reduce the risk of variceal bleeding. — They lower portal pressure by decreasing cardiac output and splanchnic vasoconstriction.
In a low‑resource setting without endoscopy, how would you screen for varices? — Use clinical risk (Child‑Pugh B/C, prior bleed) and start prophylactic propranolol in all high‑risk patients.

What distinguishes hepatorenal syndrome from acute kidney injury due to diuretics? — HRS presents with low urine sodium (< 10 mmol/L), normal renal ultrasound, and no response to fluid withdrawal; diuretic AKI improves after dose reduction.

A pregnant woman with cirrhosis presents with melena. How do you manage her bleed? — Stabilize with IV fluids, give IV octreotide if available, arrange urgent endoscopic band ligation; avoid teratogenic drugs.
Why is albumin given after large‑volume paracentesis? — To maintain intravascular oncotic pressure and prevent circulatory dysfunction.
